question: According to the October 2025 *World Economic Outlook* (WEO), what is the projected path of global headline inflation from 2024 to 2026?
gold_answer: Global headline inflation is projected to decline from 5.8% in 2024 to 4.2% in 2025 and 3.7% in 2026.
final_answer: According to the October 2025 *World Economic Outlook*, global headline inflation is projected to decline from 5.8 percent in 2024 to 4.2 percent in 2025, and further decrease to 3.7 percent in 2026. This decline is driven by factors such as cooling demand and falling energy prices. question: Why did point-to-point food inflation ease substantially during FY25 while the 12-month average remained elevated?

The 12-month average remained elevated because it still incorporated the exceptionally high inflation recorded during the first half of the fiscal year, making it a lagging indicator.

question: Combining global commodity developments and domestic CPI data, explain why Bangladesh’s inflation remained elevated in FY25 despite falling global commodity prices.
gold_answer: Although global commodity prices, particularly energy prices, declined, domestic inflation remained elevated because of supply-chain disruptions, depreciation of the Bangladeshi Taka that increased import costs, persistently high food prices, and the lingering effects of earlier inflationary shocks. These domestic factors outweighed the benefits of lower global commodity prices.
final_answer: In FY25, Bangladesh experienced an average CPI-based inflation rate of 10.03 percent, which remained elevated despite a decline in global commodity prices. This persistent inflation was primarily driven by higher food inflation, which reached 10.70 percent, and non-food inflation at 9.47 percent. Contributing factors included ongoing global commodity price shocks, increased transport and energy costs, and currency depreciation. Notably, food inflation slightly increased from 10.66 percent in June 2024 to 10.70 percent in June 2025, while non-food inflation rose from 8.86 percent to 9.47 percent during the same period. These elements collectively explain why inflation in Bangladesh stayed high in FY25, despite falling global commodity prices. question: Based on the near-term outlook, what domestic and external factors could either support or hinder further disinflation in Bangladesh in the coming period?
gold_answer: Factors supporting further disinflation include tight monetary policy, declining global commodity prices, exchange-rate stabilization, adequate rainfall, and favorable agricultural conditions. Potential obstacles include the pass-through of higher import costs from U.S. tariffs, lingering supply-side constraints, persistently elevated core inflation, renewed exchange-rate depreciation, and fiscal pressures.
final_answer:
The near-term outlook for disinflation in Bangladesh is influenced by both domestic and external factors. On the one hand, increased import costs due to escalated US-imposed tariffs may hinder further disinflation, as these costs could lead to additional inflationary pressures [Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.10][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.24][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.18][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.2][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.9]. Additionally, elevated policy and market interest rates, with the policy (repo) rate at 10.0 percent and the standing lending facility (SLF) rate at 11.5 percent, are likely to constrain private sector investment and further disinflation efforts [Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.10][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.24][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.23][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.19].

Conversely, several factors may support disinflation. Adequate rainfall and a favorable agricultural environment, along with easing global commodity prices and effective monetary policy, are expected to contribute to a gradual moderation of CPI inflation in Bangladesh over FY26, with a projected decline from 11.66 percent in July 2024 to 8.48 percent in June 2025 [Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.10][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.24][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.3][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.19][Chapter-1-2-3.pdf, p.18].
